INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1
The Cato Institute is a nonpartisan public policy
research foundation founded in 1977 and dedicated to
advancing the principles of individual liberty, free
markets, and limited government. Cato’s Project on
Criminal Justice was founded in 1999 and focuses in
particular on the scope of substantive criminal liability, the proper and effective role of police in their communities, the protection of constitutional and statutory safeguards for criminal suspects and defendants,
citizen participation in the criminal justice system,
and accountability for law enforcement officers.




1 Rule 37.6 statement: No part of this brief was authored by any
party’s counsel, and no person or entity other than amicus funded
its preparation or submission.

2


SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
Mr. Watanabe alleges that after being brutally assaulted, and while in 10-out-of-10 pain, a government
nurse told him “to stop being a cry baby” and refused
to send him to the hospital. Mr. Watanabe’s coccyx was
broken. Untreated for years, the bone chips migrated
into his soft tissue.
Mr. Watanabe says the nurse’s deliberate indifference to his serious medical need is an Eighth Amendment violation cognizable under Bivens. He filed this
suit asking for his injuries to be treated by a specialist
and damages. The Court of Appeals permitted his suit
to proceed.
The nurse disagrees. He wants the Court to grant
him—and everyone else in the federal government—
sweeping immunity from monetary damages. Page one
of his brief , in fact,  calls for this case to be “the final
installment of the Bivens saga.”
As of oral argument before the Court of Appeals,
the government had not taken Mr. Watanabe to a specialist.
ARGUMENT
Centuries of law support Mr. Watanabe’s claim for
damages. What was plain to Blackstone was incorporated into American law by the Founding Generation.
No lens of interpretation —be it originalism, textualism, or even ordinary statutory interpretation —indicates otherwise.
Petitioner would have this Court rewrite  these
basic principles. His view, if adopted, would render
hollow history and precedent, exacerbating the chasm
between favored and disfavored constitutional rights

3


that this Court has been trying to bridge for decades.
It is an invitation to engage in policymaking—judicial
repeal rather than restraint.
The Cato Institute  respectfully asks the Court to
reject Petitioner’s invitation.
This brief first explains why settled law supports
Mr. Watanabe’s claim. History, text, and precedent all
point toward the traditional remedy : monetary damages against the individual who violated the plaintiff’s
rights. Because the Constitution already incorporated
the tradition of damages in courts of law, the parties’
statutory interpretation arguments are avoidable.
Should the Court find it necessary or helpful to look
at the statutory debate, this brief next shows the ways
in which Congress has implicitly blessed if not expressly approved suits seeking damages against federal officers.
Lastly, this brief seeks to convey to the Court how
divorced Petitioner’s arguments are from the lived experiences of ordinary Americans . “The people themselves” know that the Constitution is already supposed
to protect them from the worst government abuses.
The Federalist No. 49. It would, candidly, be shocking
for the Court to say that a theory of constitutional organization demands further authorizing legislation.
The Court should put its foot down. The “final installment of the Bivens saga” should be a return to
founding values and constitutional text: a realization
that Bivens was never necessary in the first place. The
People who adopted the Constitution knew money
damages were available from those who wronged
them, even if they worked for the federal government.
The People of today, heirs of that tradition, cannot be

4


divested of th at established remedy without proper
amendment of the Constitution.
A. Damages Are the Default Remedy
Centuries of law indicate that money damages are
the default remedy for injured persons  who seek justice in courts of law.
Blackstone stated the  “general and indisputable
rule, that where there is a legal right, there is also a
legal remedy by suit or action at law, whenever that
right is invaded.” Marbury v. Madison, 5 U.S. 137, 163
(1803). The remedy for personal injuries was plain: a
man who is beaten “may have satisfaction by recovering equivalent damages ,” he said.  1 William Blackstone, Commentaries *131.
Monetary damages were not available from private
defendants only. Abusive government officers faced liability as well.
The authority is ancient. Before 1275, English law
provided that a government officer who acted without
authority “should pay double damages to the plaintiff,
and a heavy fine to the king, for doing injury in his
name to the subject. ” United States v. Lee, 106 U.S.
196, 229 (1882) (citing Lord Coke).
In Mostyn v. Fabrigas, for example, a British officer
was held personally liable for destroying the homes of
settlers on Nova Scotia. See 1 Cowp. 180 (1774), as discussed in Mitchell v. Harmony, 54 U.S. 115, 135
(1851). Even though the officer had acted on orders, “it
was an invasion of the rights of private property, and
without the authority of law, and the officer who executed the order was held liable to an action, and the
[settlers] recovered damages against him .” Mitchell,
54 U.S. at 136.

5


The Founding Generation knew this principle.
In 1787, for example, Anti-Federalists supported
the nascent Seventh Amendment by pointing to a substantial damages award issued against an officer who
had engaged in an “outrageous search.” Charles W.
Wolfram, The Constitutional History of the Seventh
Amendment, 57 Minn. L. Rev.  639, 708 (1973). It was
taken for granted that if “the military officers of Congress, by a wanton abuse of power, imprison the free
citizens of the United States of America ,” the author
wrote, or “a constable, having a warrant to search for
stolen goods, pulled down the clothes of a bed in which
there was a woman and searched under her shift ,”
then “ heavy damages would at once punish the offender and deter others from committing the same .”
Id. at 708 n.187.
The jurists of the Founding Generation knew this
principle too. They applied it faithfully, even despite
initial hesitation.
In Little v. Barreme, the plaintiff sought money
damages from an American ship captain who seized a
Danish vessel pursuant to an unlawful order of the
president. 6 U.S. 170 (1804), summarized in Hencely v.
Fluor Corp., 608 U.S. 31, 146 S. Ct. 1086, 1098 (2026).
The U.S. district court let the captain off the hook for
damages, and Chief Justice Marshall was (at first)
prone to agree. “[T]he first bias of my mind was” to “excuse from damages” the captain, he admitted . 6 U.S.
at 179. “ But I have been convinced that I was mistaken” by “my brethren,” he wrote. Id. Under ordinary
operation of law, this Court held, the captain “must be
answerable in damages.” Id.

6


In short, for centuries, government officers who violated people’s rights were personally liable for monetary damages. E.g., Tracy v. Swartwout, 35 U.S. 80,
98–99 (1836)  (“Some personal inconvenience may be
experienced by an officer who shall be held responsible
in damages for illegal acts done under instructions of
a superior; but, as the government in such cases is
bound to indemnify the officer, there can be no eventual h ardship.”); Mitchell, 54 U.S. at 130 (affirming
damages award against federal officers) ; see also Stephen I. Vladeck, The Inconsistent Originalism of
Judgemade Remedies Against Federal Officers , 96
Notre Dame L. Rev. 1869, 1880 (2021).
Petitioner attempts to avoid the default remedy by
claiming that most suits invoked state law, rather
than federal law. Opening Brief at 4–5. But those were
simply “pleading conventions” used by “the lawyers of
the time .” Alfred Hill, Constitutional Remedies , 69
Colum. L. Rev. 1109, 1129 (1969) . “The common law
forms of action prevailed in the state courts as a matter of historic continuity, and in the federal court[s] because Congress had directed conformity with the practice of the state courts.” Id. at 1151. In a constitutional
tort, however, “ it was nevertheless the Constitution
that determined the outcome.” Id. at 1133.
Professor Akhil Amar’s formulation is functionally
identical. “The structure of these pre-Bivens cases was
quite simple: The ultimate issue before the court concerned the federal Constitution  * * * .” Akhil Reed
Amar, Of Sovereignty and Federalism , 96 Yale L.J.
1425, 1506 (1987). They proceeded in traditional serveand-volley form:
Plaintiff would sue defendant federal officer in
trespass; defendant would claim federal

7


empowerment that trumped the state law of
trespass under the principles of the supremacy
clause; and plaintiff, by way of reply, would
play an even higher supremacy clause trump:
Any federal empowerment was ultra vires and
void because of Fourth Amendment limitations
on federal power itself.
Id. at 1506–07. To prevail on a damages claim required
plaintiff to establish “that the Fourth Amendment had
been violated,” which meant “defendant’s shield of federal power would dissolve, and he would stand as a naked tortfeasor.” Id. at 1507.
No matter the pleading convention of the era, then,
damages remedies have always been available against
individual federal officers. Petitioner would have this
Court bring centuries of tradition to an end.
Petitioner pivots, saying Mr. Watanabe “could (and
did) seek nonmonetary relief.” Opening Brief at 2. Set
aside for a moment the chutzpah it takes to advance
that argument on this record , where the government
had not provided any nonmonetary relief even as of
oral argument in the Court of Appeals. It simply is not
true that damages and injunctive relief are mutually
exclusive remedies. In Little, for example,  this Court
held that the injured party was entitled to a court order “direct[ing] a restoration of the vessel and cargo ”
and damages against the responsible officer. 6 U.S. at
176.
It is telling that Petitioner acknowledg es federal
courts’ equitable power to issue injunctions. Opening
Brief at 5. On this, amicus agrees. But consider for a
moment how federal courts obtained that power.

8


The power of injunctive relief was vested in the judiciary when the People ratified Article III, section 2:
“The judicial Power shall extend to all Cases, in Law
and Equity, arising under this Constitution  * * * .”
Courts of equity, of course, have the power to issue injunctions. E.g., Trump v. Cook, 609 U.S. ---, 146 S. Ct.
2234, 2250 (2026); Ex parte Young, 209 U.S. 123, 156
(1908). The Constitution therefore did not need more
text granting federal courts the power to issue injunctions. The word “injunction” does not appear because
it was encompassed by the word “Equity.”
The problem with Petitioner’s argument is that the
same clause of the Constitution also extends the judicial power to all cases “in Law.” An award of damages
“is the traditional form of relief offered in the courts of
law.” Curtis v. Loether, 415 U.S. 189, 196  (1974) (emphasis added); see also Suja A. Thomas, A Limitation
on Congress: “In Suits at Common Law ”, 71 Ohio St.
L.J. 1071, 1074 (2010) . So the Constitution did not
need to add the word “damages” to make the remedy
available. It was encompassed by the word “Law.”
Petitioner does not mention this text. He does not
cite Article III at all, in fact. But that is the place
where the remedy of damages was incorporated into
the Constitution. And just as equity does not require
“a congressionally-provided cause of action to prevent
an injurious act by a public officer,” Trump, 146 S. Ct.
at 2251 n.2 (emphasis added), law does not require a
congressionally-provided cause of action to make that
person whole after an injury.
Congress cannot, by its inaction, exempt federal
employees from the reach of the Eighth Amendment.
“Constitutional rights are enshrined with the scope
they were understood to have when the people adopted

9


them.” Dist. of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 634
(2008). That enumeration “ takes out of the hands of
government”—be it the Legislative or Judicial Branch
of Government—“the power to decide on a case-by-case
basis whether the right is really worth insisting upon.”
Id.; see also  N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n, Inc. v.
Bruen, 597 U.S. 1, 23 (2022) (same); McDonald v. City
of Chicago, 561 U.S. 742, 791 (2010) (same). The principle is as true for the Eighth Amendment as it is for
the Second.2
*  *  *
History and text point in the same direction: the
Constitution incorporates an 800-year-old tradition establishing money damages as the default remedy for a
government official’s violation of rights. Congressional
action or inaction cannot change that. Petitioner’s favored remedy must await proposal and ratification as
set forth in Article V.


2 There is no good reason to limit this rationale to Second Amendment cases. The Eighth Amendment is no less worthy of respect
than its brethren : there are no “second class” constitutional
rights. And the Eighth Amendment is no less rooted in history
than the right to bear arms. “In fact, the entire text of the Eighth
Amendment is taken almost verbatim from the English Declaration of Rights” of 1689, which itself was based upon “the knowne
Lawes and Statutes and Freedome of this Realme.” Harmelin v.
Michigan, 501 U.S. 957, 966, 969 (1991).

10


B. Congress Ratified and Never Repudiated
the Availability of Damages
Should constitutional text, history, and tradition
fail to persuade, the Court may also ground Mr.
Watanabe’s damages remedy in the actions of the legislative branch.
Congress has repeatedly legislated on —and ratified—the premise that the Bivens action exists. Congress has legislated three times on the express understanding that damages actions against individual federal officers exist.
First, the FTCA (1946) supplemented the officer
suit with a claim against the United States itself. It
displaced nothing; officer liability continued as before.
See James E. Pfander & Rex N. Alley, Federal Tort Liability After Egbert v. Boule : The Case for Restoring
the Officer Suit at Common Law , 138 Harv. L. Rev.
985, 1034 (2025)  (discussing Carlson v. Green, 446
U.S. 14, 33 (1980) ); see also 28 U.S.C. § 2676 (FTCA
judgment bar expressly contemplating existence of
simultaneous claim against individual officers).
Second, after federal agents ’ notorious wrong -
house raids in Collinsville, Illinois, Congress enacted
the 1974 law-enforcement proviso, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(h),
waiving sovereign immunity for intentional torts by
federal law enforcement officers. See Martin v. United
States, 605 U.S. 395, 419 –20 (2025) (Sotomayor, J.,
concurring). The accompanying committee report
“made it crystal clear that Congress views FTCA and
Bivens as parallel, complementary causes of action. ”
Carlson, 446 U.S. at 19 –20. In Congress’s own words:
“after the date of enactment of this measure, innocent
individuals who are subjected to raids [like that in

11


Bivens] will have a cause of action against the individual Federal agents and the Federal Government,” and
the provision “should be viewed as a counterpart to the
Bivens case and its progen[y]. ” Id. at 20  (quoting S.
Rep. No. 93-588, at 3 (1973)).
Third, the Westfall Act (1988)  decisively ref lects
congressional approval of Bivens. After Westfall v. Erwin, Congress let ordinary negligence claims against
federal employees proceed only against the United
States, § 2679(b)(1), but expressly carved out and preserved constitutional claims against individual officers, § 2679(b)(2)(A). The exclusivity provisions do not
apply to any “civil action against an employee of the
Government * * * which is brought for a violation of
the Constitution of the United States.” 28 U.S.C. §
2679(b)(2)(A).
The carveout is intelligible only as ratification:
Congress altered the administration of negligence
claims while preserving the traditional remedy for constitutional claims. See Carlos M. Vázquez & Stephen
I. Vladeck, State Law, the Westfall Act, and the Nature
of the Bivens Question, 161 U. Pa. L. Rev. 509 (2013) .
A Congress that believed damages suits against federal officers for unconstitutional conduct illegitimate
does not write a statutory safe harbor for those suits.
Courts enforce the ordinary meaning of statutes.
E.g., Schindler Elevator Corp. v. U.S. ex rel. Kirk, 563
U.S. 401, 407 (2011) . A Court that is faithful to Congressional text interprets the law to “ ensure that the
statutory scheme is coherent and consistent” and cannot “ rewrite the statute to reflect a meaning [it]
deem[s] more desirable.” Ali v. Fed. Bureau of Prisons,
552 U.S. 214, 222, 227 (2008) (reinstating FTCA claim
in BOP context). Here, that means Petitioner cannot

12


wave away congressional protection of constitutional
damages actions. Cf. Bufkin v. Collins, 604 U.S. 369,
386 (2025) (“We are reluctant to treat statutory terms
as surplusage in any setting. Our reluctance increases
when Congress amends a statute * * * .”).
Petitioner’s brief nevertheless describes “grave separation-of-powers concerns” if the  Bivens remedy is
permitted to continue in present form. Opening Brief
at 32. He wants the Court to believe that Congress has
“to step into the field itself.” Id. at 17. Yet Congress
already has. Petitioner would require the Court to turn
a blind eye to all the things that Congress did to
streamline the traditional remedy by accommodating
parallel Bivens claims.
The full understanding of statutory history disproves the tale of Bivens as lawless judicial improvisation. If Bivens broke new ground it simply collapsed
the Founding Era two -step—common-law writ, then
constitutional reply—into a single claim arising under
the Constitution itself, so that the constitutional violation that once defeated the officer’s justification argument now states the cause of action directly. See Amar,
supra, at 1506–07; James E. Pfander & David Baltmanis, Rethinking Bivens: Legitimacy and Constitutional
Adjudication, 98 Geo. L.J. 117, 121 (2009)  (proposing
that courts treat the Bivens action as presumptively
available and ask only “whether Congress deliberately
displaced the Bivens remedy through the adoption of
an alternative remedial scheme”).
The full understanding of statutory history also reveals that overruling or hollowing Carlson and Bivens
would not restore some pre -1971 baseline. It would
knock out the pillar of relief Congress deliberately left
standing. That is  judicial repeal rather than true

13


respect for separation of powers concerns. It would be
a judicial rug -pull of the constitutional order and a
stark departure from the original understanding of the
remedies the People held against federal lawlessness.
And, as the below section reveals, it would further encourage federal officer impunity.
C. Unaccountability Would Not Have Been
Justifiable to the Founders —and Should
Not Be to Their Descendants
Americans tell ourselves stories of how our laws set
us apart from other systems that are insufficiently
protective of liberty, freedom, and the self -evident
truth that all men are created equal.
Our Founders were uniquely concerned with the
dangers—to liberty, freedom, and equality—presented
by an unaccountable governing class. John Adams famously intoned, “ the very definition of a Republic, is
‘an Empire of Laws, and not of Men. ’” John Adams,
Thoughts on Government  (Apr. 1776); see also Mass.
Const. pt. 1, art. XXX  (drafted by John Adams, 1780)
(“[T]o the end it may be a government of laws, and not
of men. ”). Our second president’s  second cousin said
much the same: “There shall be one rule of Justice for
rich and poor, for the favorite in Court, and the Countryman at the Plough.” Samuel Adams (for the Boston
Committee of Correspondence), The Rights of the Colonists (Nov. 20, 1772) (quoting John Locke, Two Treatises of Government).
And from the start, our judiciary recognized its role
in jealously guarding liberty, freedom, and the promise
of equality by enforcing the law even against the executive. “The very essence of civil liberty certainly consists in the right of every individual to claim the

14


protection of the laws, whenever he receives an injury.
One of the first duties of government is to afford that
protection.” Marbury, 5 U.S. at 163. This is because
“[t]he government of the United States has been emphatically termed a government of laws, and not of
men.” Id. The alternative—immunity and impunity—
would lead to universal diminishment.  “It will certainly cease to deserve this high appellation, if the
laws furnish no remedy for the violation of a vested legal right.” Id.; see also The Apollon, 22 U.S. 362, 367
(1824) (permitting damages claim against federal official for unlawful seizure: “t his Court can only look to
the questions, whether the laws have been violated;
and if they were, justice demands, that the injured
party should receive a suitable redress.”).
Even in exceptionally difficult moments, and even
for particularly disfavored plaintiffs, the federal judiciary has seen fit to provide for accountability against
federal officer misconduct.  See, e.g., Lee, 106 U.S. at
220 (affirming jury verdict for family of General Robert E. Lee finding unconstitutional conduct by federal
officials at the Department of War and elsewhere that
required return of land containing Arlington National
Cemetery).
The Lee Court’s promise of accountability sang the
same song as the Founders:
No man in this country is so high that he is
above the law. No officer of the law may set
that law at defiance with impunity. All the officers of the government, from the highest to
the lowest, are creatures of the law and are
bound to obey it. It is the o nly supreme power
in our system of government, and every man
who by accepting office participates in its

15


functions is only the more strongly bound to
submit to that supremacy, and to observe the
limitations which it imposes upon the exercise
of the authority which it gives.
Id.
In war as at peace,  there is no alternative to accountability for a government that respects freedom.
“With all its defects, delays and inconveniences, men
have discovered no technique for long preserving free
government except that the Executive be under the
law * * * .” Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer,
343 U.S. 579, 655 (1952) (Jackson, J., concurring).
Amicus respectfully submits that just as the
Founders would have been shocked to learn that federal officials are purportedly immune from accountability at law, Americans today should find such impunity inconsistent with the foundational promise and
premise of our nation . Hollowing out the only meaningful remedy ordinary Americans have when a federal officer violates the Constitution  would only exacerbate their fears, further weakening the social compact.
The end of damages suits for unconstitutional acts
of federal official s would not just be surprising, it
would have far-reaching consequences. To see why,
take a look at Bivens cases in the Courts of Appeals.
Donald Vance and Nathan Ertel plausibly alleged
that “members of the United States military tortured
them in violation of the United States Constitution ,”
in retaliation for bringing illegal arms trafficking activity to the attention of the FBI. Vance v. Rumsfeld,
701 F.3d 193, 211 (7th Cir. 2012) (en banc) (Hamilton,
dissenting). The Seventh Circuit, sitting en banc ,

16


rejected the availability of a Bivens remedy. Three
judges noted that this left no remedy for “civilian U.S.
citizens who are tortured or worse by our own military,” reflecting “a degree of hypocrisy that is breathtaking.” Id.
In 2011, Hawo Ahmed and Hamdi Mohamud were
framed by a federally deputized officer. Although they
had committed no crime, the officer knowingly lied and
fabricated evidence  against them . Ahmed v. Weyker,
984 F.3d 564, 565 (8th Cir. 2020); Mohamud v. Weyker,
No. 17-CV-2069 (JNE/TNL), 2018 WL 4469251, at *3
(D. Minn. Sept. 18, 2018). Ahmed and Mohamud were
jailed for more than two years  before the officer’s lies
unraveled. Ahmed was forced to give birth in jail before her acquittal. But the Eighth Circuit found no
Bivens remedy because, while Bivens involved an entry into a home , “[h]ere, by contrast, [the defendant
federal official] did not enter a home, even if the actions she allegedly took—like manufacturing evidence
and lying—were just as pernicious.” 984 F.3d at 568.
Kevin Byrd alleged that a Homeland Security
agent “physically threatened him with a gun,” “verbally threatened to ‘put a bullet through his f —king
skull’ and that ‘he would blow his head off,’” and “attempted to smash the window of his car.” Byrd v.
Lamb, 990 F.3d 879, 880 (5th Cir. 2021) . Surveillance
video apparently supported his claims, because after
reviewing it, local police arrested the federal agent on
charges of “aggravated assault with a deadly weapon
and misdemeanor criminal mischief.” Id. at 880 –81.
But Byrd’s claim was tossed because the force happened “in a parking lot, not a private home as was the
case in Bivens.” Id. at 882.

17


Mandriez Spivey alleged that employees of the Bureau of Prisons denied him medical care for painful
conditions and, separately, slammed his head into a
wall for something his cellmate admitted to doing.
Spivey v. Breckon, 173 F.4th 174, 176 (4th Cir. 2026) .
Spivey’s case ended because his claims were less severe than those blessed by the Bivens trilogy. The
Court of Appeals reasoned that that “ even ‘quite minor’ differences between a proposed claim and the
claims in the three existing  Bivens cases can amount
to a new context.” 173 F.4th at 180.
If proven by the evidence, all of these cases feature
constitutional violations that, under the traditional
remedy, were eligible for monetary damages. Yet all of
these plaintiffs’  claims were dismissed by the lower
courts—each of which claimed to act pursuant to this
Court’s instructions.
These cases did not rise to  national attention like
the recent ICE killings of Renée Good and Alex Pretti.
Yet they illustrate how the lower courts apply Bivens,
and in some instances how federal judges are looking
to this Court for guidance and leadership. As Judge
Willett put it, “ I am certainly not the first to express
unease that individuals whose constitutional rights
are violated at the hands of federal officers are essentially remedy-less. A written constitution is mere meringue when rights can be violated with nonchalance.”
Byrd, 990 F.3d at 884–85 (Willett, J., concurring). He
wrote to “ add my voice to those lamenting today ’s
rights-without-remedies regime, hoping (against hope)
that as the chorus grows louder, change comes sooner.”
Id. at 885.
If in this moment in history, the Court decides that
the People have no damages remedy  at law against

18


wayward federal officers, the consequences will be unpredictable and perhaps severe.3
Citizens will have less trust that the Constitution
protects them. Federal agents will have more confidence that the Constitution does not impose consequences for their lawlessness.4 There will be more excessive force and denial of medical care cases like  Mr.
Vance’s, Mr. Byrd’s, and Mr. Watanabe’s. And federal
agents will have more “freedom” to innovate with
newer forms of constitutional violations like jawboning—even those this Court has already held to be unconstitutional. See Nat’l Rifle Ass’n of Am. v. Vullo,
602 U.S. 175 (2024) (holding, in case against state officials, that “the First Amendment prohibits government officials from wielding their power selectively to
punish or suppress speech, directly or (as alleged here)
through private intermediaries.”); Murthy v. Missouri,
